```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
```

`breedtools` designs and analyses plant breeding trials, from early
generations with a single plot per entry to fully replicated trials, saves
the designs directly into a 'Breedbase' database, and helps decide which
environments can be analysed together. This tutorial goes through every
design and analysis in the package, using simulated phenotypes.

```{r setup}
library(breedtools)
```

## Which design?

| Situation | Design | Generate | Analyse |
|---|---|---|---|
| Seed for one plot per entry, one location | Augmented row-column design with replicated checks | `augmented_row_column_design()` | `analyze_augmented_row_column_design()` |
| Seed for one plot per entry per location, several locations | Augmented p-rep design (part of the entries repeated at each location, no checks needed) | `augmented_prep_design()` | `analyze_augmented_prep_design()`, `analyze_augmented_prep_two_stage()` |
| Seed for every entry in every replicate | Resolvable (spatial) row-column design | `resolvable_row_column_design()` | `analyze_resolvable_row_column()` |
| Phenotypes from several trials in 'Breedbase' | Variance check and environment grouping | `run_breedbase_variance_check()`, `run_environment_stratification()` | |
| A design ready to plant | Save it as a trial in a 'Breedbase' program and folder | `save_breedbase()` | |

Every design function returns a list with `summary`, the plot-level `design`
(the field book) and `breedbase_design` (the columns for a 'Breedbase'
upload), and accepts `seed` for a reproducible randomization and
`output_file` for a tab-delimited copy. Every analysis returns adjusted
entry means (`adjusted_means`) ranked best first, with standard errors, the
mean standard error of a difference (`mean_sed`) and the 5% least
significant difference (`lsd_5pct`).

## Start with the information you know

Use `design_options()` when you know how many entries you have but have
not settled on the field dimensions, number of checks or replication.
It proposes layouts for augmented row-column, p-rep and fully replicated
resolvable row-column designs:

```{r design-options}
options <- design_options(n_entries = 100, n_locations = 3)
options[, c("option", "design", "n_checks", "rows_in_field", "cols_in_field", "n_reps",
             "plots_per_location", "error_df")]
```

`n_entries` counts test entries, excluding checks. To consider only certain
designs, use `design = c("augmented_row_column", "resolvable")`, for example. Supply
known constraints and leave the others unspecified:

```{r constrained-design-options}
fixed_options <- design_options(108, design = "augmented_row_column", n_checks = 4,
  rows_in_field = 12, cols_in_field = 12, n_candidates = 200)
fixed_options[, c("option", "rows_in_field", "cols_in_field", "rows_per_block",
                   "cols_per_block", "n_candidates", "check_plots", "error_df", "method")]
design_options(42, design = "resolvable", cols_in_field = 7, n_reps = 3)
```

`rows_in_field` and `cols_in_field` describe the entire field at one
location, including all checks and replicates; block dimensions are
suggested in the result as `rows_per_block` and `cols_per_block`. A
supplied dimension is an exact candidate size; a vector such as
`rows_in_field = c(12, 15, 18)` considers each size. When possible,
the first augmented row-column option has square blocks of `n_checks` rows
by `n_checks` columns, such as 3 x 3 blocks for three checks. `max_plots` limits field area
per location. `unused_plots` reports filler positions or a partial final
row. `min_error_df = 10`, for example, can exclude layouts with little
nominal error information. `attr(options, "diagnostics")` explains why a
requested design family has no options within the search limits.

Choose an augmented row-column option and pass every setting explicitly to
`augmented_row_column_design()`. This design family is identified by
`"augmented_row_column"`; the shorter name `"augmented"` is not used.
The planner requires at least one block row and one block column per
distinct check: with four checks, every suggested block is at least
4 rows by 4 columns. This leaves room for one copy of each check in a
distinct row and column of the block.

```{r generate-planned-design}
selected <- fixed_options[1, ]
entries <- sprintf("LINE_%03d", 1:108)
check_names <- c("CHECK_A", "CHECK_B", "CHECK_C", "CHECK_D")
planned_trial <- augmented_row_column_design(
  treatments       = entries,
  controls         = check_names,
  rows_in_field    = selected$rows_in_field,
  cols_in_field    = selected$cols_in_field,
  rows_per_block   = selected$rows_per_block,
  cols_per_block   = selected$cols_per_block,
  checks_per_block = selected$checks_per_block[[1]],
  method           = selected$method,
  n_candidates     = selected$n_candidates,
  seed             = 2026
)
check_design(planned_trial)
```

`n_candidates = 200` is the search effort you choose. The planner suggests
the dimensions and block arrangement; it records your chosen search effort
alongside them. Include `checks_per_block` because options that need extra
check replication carry that allocation in this column. It is `NULL` for
complete blocks with one copy of every check.

For other design families, `selected$arguments[[1]]` supplies their layout
arguments for `do.call()`. For p-rep, replace the placeholder locations with your location
names. For resolvable designs, include both entries and checks in
the generator's `treatments`; both are fully replicated. The native resolvable
generator needs checks marked in `is_control` in its two field-book tables
if check status is needed for Breedbase.

The planner checks counts, block conditions and nominal error degrees of
freedom. It does not randomize a design or estimate its precision. Generate
your selected option and inspect its summary and `check_design()` results
to assess connectivity and efficiency. Extra positions in augmented
layouts are assigned explicitly to extra check replication, keeping the
number of test entries exact.

A longer script that you can run section by section in RStudio ships with
the package:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
file.edit(system.file("examples", "breedtools_workflow.R", package = "breedtools"))
```

# 1. Augmented row-column designs

Unreplicated entries are tested together with a few replicated checks. Rows
and columns are grouped into row groups and column groups, and each
intersection is a block that receives check plots. Row, column and block
effects are estimated from the checks and used to adjust the entries
(Federer, Nair and Raghavarao, 1975; Piepho and Williams, 2016).

## Plan the layout

Row, column and block effects are estimated from the check plots only, so a
layout must leave error degrees of freedom after estimating them. Check this
before you plant:

```{r}
augmented_row_column_capacity(
  rows_in_field = 12, cols_in_field = 12,
  rows_per_block = 4, cols_per_block = 4,
  n_controls = 4
)
```

`entry_plots` is the number of test entries that fit, and `error_df` must be
positive (Clarke and Stefanova, 2011, recommend about 50 when the field is
large enough). `min_rowgroup_slack` and `min_colgroup_slack` are the
conditions of Piepho and Williams (2016) for the row-group and column-group
sub-designs; negative values warn that those sub-designs cannot be
estimated on their own.

`augmented_row_column_layouts()` lists analyzable layouts whose blocks have
at least as many rows and columns as checks, most entry plots first, so you
can see the trade-off between entry plots and error df. Give `n_entries`
to keep only the layouts that fit your
entries, and `min_error_df` to require a minimum precision:

```{r}
augmented_row_column_layouts(rows_in_field = 12, cols_in_field = 12, n_controls = 2:5)
augmented_row_column_layouts(12, 12, n_controls = 2:6, min_error_df = 6, n_entries = 100)
```

`method` shows which construction `augmented_row_column_design()` will use
for the layout (see below).

## Generate and inspect

```{r}
rc <- augmented_row_column_design(
  treatments = sprintf("LINE_%03d", 1:108),
  controls = c("CHECK_A", "CHECK_B", "CHECK_C", "CHECK_D"),
  rows_in_field = 12, cols_in_field = 12,
  rows_per_block = 4, cols_per_block = 4,
  n_candidates = 200,
  seed = 2026
)
rc$summary[, c("method", "total_plots", "check_plots", "entry_plots",
               "error_df", "d_criterion")]
head(rc$design)
```

For regular layouts like this one, checks are placed with covering Latin
rectangles (`method = "latin"`): each block holds one plot of each check,
checks never share a row or column within a block, and every field row and
column contains a check:

```{r}
checks <- rc$design[rc$design$is_control == 1, ]
table(checks$all_entries, checks$block)
all(1:12 %in% checks$row) && all(1:12 %in% checks$col)
```

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plot_augmented_row_column_design(rc, label = "all_entries", fill = "type")
```

`check_design()` runs the standard checks of any design and prints one
`[OK]` or `[FAIL]` line per check; it works the same way for p-rep and
resolvable row-column designs. Add checks of your own with
`check_result()`, and count them with `check_summary()`:

```{r}
check_design(rc)
check_result("all 108 entries in the field book", sum(rc$design$is_control == 0) == 108)
check_summary()
```

## Flexible layouts (Piepho and Williams, 2016)

Row and column groups need not be equal, and blocks can hold fewer check
plots than there are checks (incomplete blocks) or more (extra replication).
Such layouts use `method = "optimal"`: check labels are allocated to blocks
in a balanced way and the check plots are then placed by a local search that
maximizes the D-criterion of the check-plot model, with spatial spread as a
tie-breaker. This reproduces Example 3 of Piepho and Williams (2016): 173
entries and 4 checks on 22 rows and 10 columns, with blocks of 3 to 5 check
plots.

```{r}
pb <- rbind(c(4, 5, 4), c(3, 5, 3), c(3, 5, 4), c(3, 5, 3))
augmented_row_column_capacity(
  n_controls = 4,
  rows_per_rowgroup = c(6, 5, 6, 5),
  cols_per_colgroup = c(3, 4, 3),
  checks_per_block = pb
)[, c("total_plots", "check_plots", "entry_plots", "error_df")]

ex3 <- augmented_row_column_design(
  treatments = paste0("E", 1:173),
  controls = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  rows_per_rowgroup = c(6, 5, 6, 5),
  cols_per_colgroup = c(3, 4, 3),
  checks_per_block = pb,
  n_candidates = 3,
  seed = 1
)
ex3$summary[, c("method", "error_df", "d_criterion")]
table(ex3$design$block[ex3$design$is_control == 1])
```

```{r, fig.height = 7}
plot_augmented_row_column_design(ex3, label = "type", fill = "type")
```

A single number in `checks_per_block` gives the same number of check plots
in every block. With 6 checks and 5 check plots per block, every block is an
incomplete block of checks:

```{r}
incomplete <- augmented_row_column_design(
  treatments = paste0("E", 1:279), controls = paste0("C", 1:6),
  rows_in_field = 18, cols_in_field = 18, rows_per_block = 6, cols_per_block = 6,
  checks_per_block = 5, n_candidates = 2, seed = 1
)
incomplete$summary[, c("method", "check_plots", "entry_plots", "error_df")]
```

Both methods follow the same placement rules as the paper's designs: no
check plots next to each other inside a block, every check in a block (or
column, or row) that has room for all checks, and even numbers of check plots
in the rows and columns of each group. For regular layouts the Latin
construction is fast and usually at least as D-efficient; `method =
"optimal"` is used for layouts it cannot make (unequal groups, incomplete
blocks, extra check replication).

## Analyse

Simulate yields with a fertility gradient down the rows and a few lost plots:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
field <- rc$design
field$yield <- 60 + 0.8 * field$row - 0.3 * field$col +
  ifelse(field$is_control == 1, 5, 0) + rnorm(nrow(field), sd = 3)
field$yield[c(7, 50, 101)] <- NA

rc_fit <- analyze_augmented_row_column_design(field, response = "yield")
rc_fit
```

The model is that of Piepho and Williams (2016, Eq. 1): row groups, rows
within row groups, column groups, columns within column groups, blocks and
genotypes. The ANOVA degrees of freedom are those estimable from the
observed plots, so the F-tests stay valid with missing plots.

`rc_fit$adjusted_means` ranks the genotypes by their adjusted mean (BLUE):
the expected value of the genotype in an average plot of the field. For an
unreplicated entry, this is its plot value corrected for the row, column and
block effects of that plot, as estimated from the checks. Rank and select on
these, not on the raw values:

```{r}
head(rc_fit$adjusted_means)
rc_fit$diagnostics[, c("anova_error_df", "sigma", "mean_sed", "lsd_5pct")]
```

`std_error` includes the uncertainty in the spatial correction. With only a
few error df, as here, that uncertainty is large, which is a reason to prefer
layouts with more check plots.

## Mixed and spatial analyses

When blocks are not complete replicates of the checks, treating rows,
columns and blocks as random recovers inter-block information
(`random_blocks = TRUE`). Entries from one breeding population can also be
modelled as random with the checks fixed (`entries = "random"`), which gives
BLUPs. Both are fitted by REML with 'lme4'; the ANOVA table is always the
fixed-effects table.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)}
rc_random <- analyze_augmented_row_column_design(field, response = "yield",
                                                 random_blocks = TRUE)
rc_random$variance_components
rc_blup <- analyze_augmented_row_column_design(field, response = "yield",
                                               random_blocks = TRUE,
                                               entries = "random")
head(rc_blup$adjusted_means)
rc_blup$message
```

A smooth two-dimensional P-spline surface over the field can be added as a
spatial component with 'SpATS' (`spatial = TRUE`); rows, columns and blocks
are then random:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("SpATS", quietly = TRUE)}
rc_spatial <- analyze_augmented_row_column_design(field, response = "yield",
                                                  spatial = TRUE)
rc_spatial$diagnostics[, c("model_type", "mean_sed", "spatial_effective_dim")]
```

Compare `mean_sed` between the fixed, mixed and spatial fits to see which
model gives the most precise comparisons for your trial.

# 2. Augmented p-rep designs

In a multi-location trial without checks, every entry is planted once at
every location, and a subset of the entries is repeated at each location to
estimate the error and the block effects (Williams, Piepho and Whitaker,
2011). Typically every entry is repeated at exactly one location.

## Generate

```{r}
prep <- augmented_prep_design(
  treatments = sprintf("G%03d", 1:120),
  locations = c("North", "Central", "South"),
  block_size = 10,
  prep_prop = 0.2,
  field_cols = 10,
  n_candidates = 200,
  seed = 2026
)
prep$summary[, c("n_locations", "n_entries", "n_plots", "n_blocks",
                 "max_pairwise_concurrence", "n_disconnected_locations",
                 "efficiency_factor")]
table(table(prep$design$all_entries))
```

Each location gets 20% of the entries as extra plots. The design search
(`method = "search"`, the default):

* spreads the p-rep plots evenly over the blocks;
* places them so that they connect all blocks of a location, so each
  location can also be analysed on its own (a warning is given when there
  are too few p-rep plots for that);
* keeps pairs of entries from sharing a block more than once
  (`max_pairwise_concurrence = 1` is a (0,1)-design);
* returns the most efficient of several optimal candidates
  (`efficiency_factor` is the average efficiency factor of the paper; compare
  it only between designs with the same number of plots).

The search accepts any proportion of p-rep entries (`prep_prop` or
`n_duplicate_per_location`, which can differ between locations), more than
two plots per repeated entry (`replications_per_repeated_entry`), a fixed
number of blocks, and a resolvable layout in which each location is split
into replicates that each hold every p-rep entry once:

```{r}
prep_res <- augmented_prep_design(
  treatments = sprintf("G%03d", 1:60),
  locations = c("A", "B"),
  block_size = 8,
  n_duplicate_per_location = c(A = 18, B = 12),
  resolvable = TRUE,
  field_cols = 8,
  seed = 1
)
pp <- prep_res$design[prep_res$design$entry_type == "p_rep_entry_at_this_location", ]
table(pp$location, pp$replicate)
```

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plot_augmented_prep_design(prep, locations = "North", fill = "entry_type")
```

## Algebraic constructions

Williams, Piepho and Whitaker (2011) also give two algebraic constructions in
which every entry is duplicated at exactly one location and each location is
a resolvable two-replicate design with `m` p-rep entries in every block
(final block size `(l + 1) m / 2`). `augmented_prep_parameters()` lists the
feasible settings, as in Table 3 of the paper:

```{r}
augmented_prep_parameters(n_treatments = 120, n_locations = 3, max_block_size = 10)
```

`method = "alpha"` uses partial alpha-arrays (Sections 2.1-2.2 of the paper)
and `method = "alpha2"` uses augmented alpha(2)-arrays (Section 2.4; even `m`
and an odd number of blocks per replicate). The number of p-rep entries per
block is set with `n_prep_per_block`, or chosen as the largest that fits in
`block_size`:

```{r}
prep_alpha <- augmented_prep_design(
  treatments = sprintf("G%03d", 1:120),
  locations = c("North", "Central", "South"),
  method = "alpha",
  block_size = 10,
  field_cols = 10,
  seed = 2026
)
prep_alpha2 <- augmented_prep_design(
  treatments = paste0("G", 1:42),
  locations = c("L1", "L2", "L3"),
  method = "alpha2",
  block_size = 4,
  seed = 1
)
rbind(
  search = prep$summary[, c("method", "n_plots", "n_blocks", "max_pairwise_concurrence", "efficiency_factor")],
  alpha = prep_alpha$summary[, c("method", "n_plots", "n_blocks", "max_pairwise_concurrence", "efficiency_factor")],
  alpha2 = prep_alpha2$summary[, c("method", "n_plots", "n_blocks", "max_pairwise_concurrence", "efficiency_factor")]
)
```

The `prep_alpha2` design is Example 3 of the paper: 42 entries in three
locations, each with 14 blocks of 4 plots.

## Analyse and rank

```{r}
set.seed(2)
genotype_effect <- setNames(rnorm(120, sd = 4), sprintf("G%03d", 1:120))
block_id <- interaction(prep$design$location, prep$design$block)
block_effect <- setNames(rnorm(nlevels(block_id), sd = 2), levels(block_id))

trial <- prep$design
trial$yield <- 50 + c(North = 0, Central = 8, South = -5)[trial$location] +
  block_effect[as.character(block_id)] +
  genotype_effect[trial$all_entries] + rnorm(nrow(trial), sd = 3)

prep_fit <- analyze_augmented_prep_design(trial, response = "yield")
prep_fit
```

The model is `location + block(location) + genotype`; for resolvable designs
replicates within locations are added and blocks are nested in replicates.
Adjusted means correct for the location and block of every plot. Because
the data are simulated, we can check that they track the true genotype
effects more closely than the raw means do:

```{r}
means <- prep_fit$adjusted_means
c(
  raw = cor(means$raw_mean, genotype_effect[means$genotype]),
  adjusted = prediction_accuracy(prep_fit, genotype_effect)
)
```

`prediction_accuracy()` is the correlation between the adjusted means and
the true values; use `method = "spearman"` to measure how well the ranking is
recovered.

Each location can also be analysed on its own (the paper's per-location
incomplete-block analysis), because the design keeps every location
connected:

```{r}
north <- analyze_augmented_prep_design(trial[trial$location == "North", ], response = "yield")
north$anova_formatted
```

## Genotype-by-location interaction

When locations are a sample of environments, add the interaction back at the
analysis stage. `genotype_by_location = "random"` fits it as a random effect
by REML (with 'lme4') and reports the variance components;
`genotype_by_location = "fixed"` fits it as a fixed effect, so the error
comes from the p-rep entries only.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)}
prep_gxl <- analyze_augmented_prep_design(trial, response = "yield",
                                          genotype_by_location = "random")
prep_gxl$variance_components
```

```{r}
prep_gxl_fixed <- analyze_augmented_prep_design(trial, response = "yield",
                                                genotype_by_location = "fixed")
prep_gxl_fixed$anova_formatted
```

## Two-stage analysis: heterogeneous variances and spatial trends

Locations rarely have the same error variance, and fields often have smooth
fertility trends. `analyze_augmented_prep_two_stage()` first analyses every
location on its own (stage 1), then combines the location means weighted by
their precision with a REML genotype-by-location variance (stage 2; Möhring
and Piepho, 2009), so noisy locations count less:

```{r}
trial_het <- trial
noisy <- trial_het$location == "South"
trial_het$yield[noisy] <- trial_het$yield[noisy] + rnorm(sum(noisy), sd = 6)

two <- analyze_augmented_prep_two_stage(trial_het, response = "yield")
two
```

`weighting = "full"` (default) uses the full covariance of the stage-1
means, `"diagonal"` only their variances, and `"none"` an unweighted
analysis:

```{r}
two_diag <- analyze_augmented_prep_two_stage(trial_het, response = "yield", weighting = "diagonal")
two_none <- analyze_augmented_prep_two_stage(trial_het, response = "yield", weighting = "none")
# Correlation with the true genotype values (known because the data are simulated):
c(full = prediction_accuracy(two, genotype_effect),
  diagonal = prediction_accuracy(two_diag, genotype_effect),
  none = prediction_accuracy(two_none, genotype_effect))
```

With `stage1 = "spatial"`, each location is fitted with a two-dimensional
P-spline surface over rows and columns using the 'SpATS' package; this needs
the field coordinates from `field_cols`:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("SpATS", quietly = TRUE)}
two_spatial <- analyze_augmented_prep_two_stage(trial_het, response = "yield",
                                                stage1 = "spatial")
two_spatial$locations[, c("location", "residual_variance", "spatial_effective_dim")]
```

## Trait plots, outliers and two-stage analysis for any design

Before the analysis, look at the trait and remove outliers. `plot_trait()`
draws a histogram and a field map per location; `remove_outliers()` applies
the IQR rule (values beyond \eqn{Q_1 - 1.5\,IQR} or \eqn{Q_3 + 1.5\,IQR},
within each location), sets them to `NA` and lists every plot and value
removed:

```{r}
sites <- c("North", "South")
met <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(i) {
  d <- augmented_row_column_design(paste0("G", 1:108), paste0("C", 1:4), 12, 12, 4, 4,
                                   n_candidates = 5, seed = i)$design
  d$location <- sites[i]
  d
}))
set.seed(4)
g <- setNames(rnorm(112, sd = 3), c(paste0("G", 1:108), paste0("C", 1:4)))
met$yield <- 50 + g[met$all_entries] + 0.6 * met$row + rnorm(nrow(met))
met$yield[10] <- 500                      # a typing error
plot_trait(met, "yield")
clean <- remove_outliers(met, "yield")
```

`analyze_two_stage()` analyses every location on its own (stage 1: a SpATS
spatial model, or the design's own model with `stage1 = "design"`) and
combines the locations weighted by their precision (stage 2). It works for
augmented row-column, p-rep and resolvable row-column designs.
`compare_first_stage()` shows how the first stage changed the plot values:

```{r}
two <- analyze_two_stage(clean, "yield", stage1 = "design")
two
cmp <- compare_first_stage(two)
```

## Single-stage analysis as an alternative

To fit all locations in one model, pass the cleaned plot observations
directly to `analyze_single_stage()`. This route does not require
`analyze_two_stage()` or any first-stage fit. Here `clean` is the
multi-location field data prepared above:

```{r single-stage-alternative}
one <- analyze_single_stage(
  clean, "yield", genotype_col = "all_entries", location_col = "location",
  spatial = requireNamespace("SpATS", quietly = TRUE)
)
one
one$variance_components
single_values <- second_stage_values(one, trait = "fresh root yield")
head(single_values)
```

`second_stage_values()` formats the genotype means of either kind of fit;
it performs no additional analysis. The single-stage model shares one
residual variance across locations, while the weighted two-stage route
uses the precision estimated at each location. Save the single-stage
means as their own analysis project:

```{r single-stage-save, eval = FALSE}
save_breedbase_analysis(single_values, con, analysis_name = "MET_2026_single_stage",
  program = "IITA", description = "Single-stage analysis of all field plots",
  estimate = if (isTRUE(one$input$spatial)) "spatial" else "blue")
```

# 3. Resolvable row-column designs

When there is enough seed to replicate every entry, a resolvable row-column
design places each treatment once in every replicate of `k` rows and `s`
columns (Williams, John and Whitaker, 2006). The search first maximizes the
average efficiency factor of the row-column design and of its row and
column components, then the spatial efficiency factor of the
two-dimensional linear variance (LV + RC) model, which spreads treatments
over neighbours and edge plots without needing prior values for spatial
parameters. `latinize = TRUE` builds a latinized design for contiguous
replicates, so that no treatment appears twice in a long column.

```{r}
rrc <- resolvable_row_column_design(
  treatments = paste0("T", 1:42),
  n_reps = 3,
  rows_per_rep = 6,
  cols_per_rep = 7,
  latinize = TRUE,
  n_starts = 1,
  seed = 1
)
rrc$summary[, c("efficiency_rc", "efficiency_rows", "efficiency_cols",
                "efficiency_spatial", "upper_bound_spatial", "latin_ok")]
```

```{r, fig.height = 7}
plot_resolvable_row_column_design(rrc)
```

Other options: replicates placed side by side
(`replicate_layout = "horizontal"`, giving long rows), t-latinized designs
(`latin_t`, latinization within groups of `t` adjacent replicates), and
fewer treatments than plots per replicate (the remaining plots become
fillers, as in Example 1 of the paper with 59 provenances in replicates of
60 plots):

```{r}
provenances <- resolvable_row_column_design(
  treatments = paste0("P", 1:59), n_reps = 4, rows_per_rep = 6, cols_per_rep = 10,
  latinize = TRUE, n_starts = 1, n_iter = 2000, seed = 1
)
provenances$summary[, c("n_treatments", "n_fillers", "efficiency_rc",
                        "efficiency_spatial", "latin_ok")]
```

## Evaluate a design

`resolvable_row_column_efficiency()` evaluates any resolvable row-column
design, including one produced elsewhere: the efficiency factors, the
spatial upper bound, treatment neighbours and edge positions, and, given
assumed parameters, the average pairwise variance under an autoregressive
model (the criterion used in Section 4 of the paper to compare designs):

```{r}
eff <- resolvable_row_column_efficiency(
  rrc, ar = list(eta_r = 35, eta_c = 60, psi = 10, rho_r = 0.5, rho_c = 0.5)
)
eff[c("efficiency_rc", "efficiency_spatial", "upper_bound_spatial", "ar_criterion")]
head(eff$neighbours)
```

An existing design (for example from CycDesigN) can be laid out, exported
and analysed with `start_design`; with `n_iter = 1` and `spatial = FALSE`
it is kept as it is:

```{r}
kept <- resolvable_row_column_design(paste0("T", 1:42), 3, 6, 7,
                                     start_design = rrc$design,
                                     n_iter = 1, spatial = FALSE)
all.equal(kept$summary$efficiency_rc, rrc$summary$efficiency_rc)
```

## Analyse

`analyze_resolvable_row_column()` fits, by REML, the standard row-column
mixed model (`model = "rc"`: replicates and treatments fixed, rows and
columns within replicates random), the two-dimensional linear variance model
(`"lv"`, LV + RC) and rows and columns plus a separable AR1 x AR1 process
(`"ar"`, AR + RC). With `compare = TRUE` (default) the sequence of models is
compared by REML deviance, the paper's way of deciding whether spatial terms
are needed. For latinized designs, the long columns can be fitted as fixed
effects (`long_col`):

```{r}
set.seed(3)
rrc_trial <- rrc$design
rrc_trial$y <- 20 + 2 * sin(rrc_trial$row / 3) + rnorm(nrow(rrc_trial))
rrc_fit <- analyze_resolvable_row_column(rrc_trial, response = "y", model = "lv",
                                         long_col = "long_col")
rrc_fit$model_comparison[, c("model", "n_variance_parameters", "deviance", "AIC", "lrt_p_value")]
rrc_fit$variance_parameters
head(rrc_fit$adjusted_means)
```

`row_variance` and `column_variance` are the variance components of rows and
columns within replicates. `equal_phi = TRUE` uses one spatial parameter for
rows and columns (square plots), and `lv_terms` adds the row-column
interaction term `phi_rc`.

# 4. Multi-environment trials from 'Breedbase'

Before combining trials, check that their error variances are similar and
group environments with a similar ranking of genotypes. The package ships
an example 'Breedbase' phenotype file with four trials.

```{r}
pheno_file <- system.file("extdata", "breedbase_pheno.csv", package = "breedtools")
raw <- read_breedbase_file(pheno_file)
dim(raw)
table(raw$locationName)
```

`read_breedbase_file()` reads `.csv`, `.txt`, `.xls` and `.xlsx` files (all
non-empty sheets of a workbook are combined). Column names are detected
automatically; `prepare_breedbase_pheno()` selects the trait and the design
columns, and `analyze_environment_anova()` gives one ANOVA per environment:

```{r}
trait <- "fresh root yield|CO_334:0000013"
pheno <- prepare_breedbase_pheno(raw, trait_col = trait)
env_anova <- analyze_environment_anova(pheno)
env_anova[, c("environment", "n_genotypes", "ms_genotype", "ms_error", "mean", "cv_percent")]
```

## Homogeneity of error variances

`run_breedbase_variance_check()` applies Hartley's Fmax test (with a
simulated critical value that allows different error df) to all
environments and finds the largest groups of environments whose error
variances are compatible:

```{r}
variance_check <- run_breedbase_variance_check(pheno_file, trait_col = trait, n_sim = 20000)
variance_check$overall_hartley
variance_check$maximal_compatible_groups
```

## Grouping environments by genotype-by-environment interaction

`run_environment_stratification()` groups environments with Lin's (1982)
test: environments are grouped when their genotype-by-environment
interaction is not significant, so they rank genotypes similarly.

```{r}
strata <- run_environment_stratification(pheno_file, trait = "fresh root yield")
strata$group_summary[, c("group_id", "locations", "n_env", "ms_ge", "f_value", "p_value")]
strata$group_membership
```

With coordinates of the locations, the groups can be drawn on an
interactive map:

```{r}
locations <- read_locations(
  system.file("extdata", "breedbase_locations.csv", package = "breedtools"),
  phenotype_data = strata
)
locations
group_map <- map_environment_groups(strata, locations)
class(group_map)
```

Print `group_map` to open the 'leaflet' map. `run_environment_stratification()`
can also export the results as JSON (`export_json = TRUE, output_dir = ...`).

# 5. Field books and saving to 'Breedbase'

Every design has a plot-level field book and the columns needed to upload
the trial to 'Breedbase':

```{r}
head(prep$breedbase_design)
head(rrc$breedbase_design)
```

Write them with `utils::write.csv()`, or pass `output_file` to the design
function for a tab-delimited copy of the full design.

## Designs generated with agricolae

The workflow has three steps: generate your design with `agricolae`,
prepare it with `prepare_breedbase_trial()`, then save it with the existing
`save_breedbase()` function. Here is an RCBD (randomized complete block
design), with three complete blocks. The same preparation function also
accepts CRD, alpha and other supported agricolae designs.

Install `agricolae` with `install.packages("agricolae")` to run this example.
The treatment column in the agricolae field book takes the name of the vector passed
to the design function (`ag_accessions` here). The converter maps that
column to `all_entries`, keeps plot and block numbers, and supplies the
replicate and check indicators used by the Breedbase uploader.

```{r agricolae-conversion, eval = requireNamespace("agricolae", quietly = TRUE)}
ag_accessions <- c("G1", "G2", "G3", "CHECK_A")
ag_randomized <- agricolae::design.rcbd(ag_accessions, r = 3, seed = 2026)
head(ag_randomized$book)           # original agricolae data format

ag_design <- prepare_breedbase_trial(
  design      = ag_randomized,
  trial_name  = "RCBD_2026_Ibadan",
  year        = 2026,
  location    = "Ibadan",
  program     = "IITA",
  description = "RCBD with three complete blocks generated with agricolae",
  checks      = "CHECK_A",
  prompt      = FALSE
)
ag_design$trial                  # recorded trial information
head(ag_design$design)            # converted plot table for Breedbase

# A bare $book or zigzag() data frame needs an explicit design type:
ag_from_book <- as_breedbase_design(
  ag_randomized$book, accession = "ag_accessions",
  checks = "CHECK_A", design_type = "RCBD"
)

# Preview the trial and plots offline:
ag_payload <- save_breedbase(ag_design, dry_run = TRUE)
ag_payload$studies[[1]]
ag_payload$plots[[1]][[1]]
ag_sheet <- phenotype_template(ag_design, traits = "fresh root yield")
head(ag_sheet)
```

The prepared object contains both the converted design and its trial name,
year, location, breeding program and description. You provide those values
once. In an interactive RStudio session, calling
`prepare_breedbase_trial(ag_randomized, checks = "CHECK_A")` asks for any
missing required trial information. Named arguments with `prompt = FALSE`
make the same workflow reproducible in scripts.

Replace the example accessions, program and location with names already in
your database. Log in, check those names and save the new trial:

```{r agricolae-save, eval = FALSE}
con <- breedbase_login("https://your-breedbase.org", "your_username")
save_breedbase(ag_design, con, dry_run = TRUE)  # check names in Breedbase
ag_saved <- save_breedbase(ag_design, con)     # create trial and plots
ag_saved$trial_page
```

Preparation does not require a connection and preserves the randomization
already generated by agricolae. Add `folder = "Your folder"` when preparing
the trial, and `create_folder = TRUE` when saving if it should be created.
You can override recorded information explicitly when saving, for example
`save_breedbase(ag_design, con, trial_name = "RCBD_2027_Ibadan", year = 2027)`.

`as_breedbase_design()` remains available for conversion without trial
information, as shown above for a bare field book. CRD, RCBD, alpha, lattice, augmented block, split-plot and strip-plot types
are recognized automatically. A bare field book, including a result from
`agricolae::zigzag()`, needs `design_type`. Designs without a corresponding
Breedbase type also require an explicit compatible `design_type`; a Latin
square is not silently relabeled as RCBD.

For multiple treatment factors, select the column containing accession
names with `accession = "genotype"`. The original factors and generation
parameters remain in `ag_design$book` and `ag_design$parameters`. Saving
uploads one plot per field-book row; it does not upload other treatment
factors or recreate a main-plot/subplot hierarchy. Repeated main-plot
numbers in split-plot books become unique sequential subplot numbers.
Coordinates are uploaded only when supplied in the field book; they are
not inferred from plot numbering or a sketch.

The same workflow is included in the runnable script's section 8e
(`scripts/breedtools_script.R`) and section E5 of the packaged example:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
file.edit(system.file("examples", "breedtools_workflow.R", package = "breedtools"))
```

Part I of `scripts/validate_designs.R` starts with RCBD and lets you select
alpha with `ag_kind = "Alpha"`. It follows the full lifecycle: a
randomization at each location, explicit field coordinates, trial
preparation and upload, phenotype sheets, trait plots,
outlier removal, SpATS per location, weighted combined means and saving the
results. It uses the same save switches and Breedbase settings as the
other trial designs in that tour. Steps I1-I3 are the design-to-trial
workflow. Set `run_agricolae_analysis <- TRUE` to also run the separate
I4-I10 example with simulated phenotypes and analysis results.

## Saving a design directly to Breedbase

`save_breedbase()` creates the trial and its plots in a 'Breedbase' database
through BrAPI. In Breedbase words, a breeding program holds folders, a folder
holds trials, and a trial holds plots. Each plot is saved with its plot
number, accession, row and column, rep, block and whether it is a check. A
multi-location p-rep design becomes one trial per location.

Without a server, `dry_run = TRUE` shows exactly what would be sent:

```{r}
to_send <- save_breedbase(rc, trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan", year = 2026,
                          location = "Ibadan", dry_run = TRUE,
                          description = "Advanced yield trial of 108 lines and 4 checks, Ibadan 2026")
to_send$studies[[1]][c("studyName", "experimentalDesign")]
str(to_send$plots[[1]][[1]])
```

With your database, log in (the password is asked for in a pop-up or read
from the `BREEDBASE_PASSWORD` environment variable; never write it in a
script), look up the names, make a dry run, and save:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
con <- breedbase_login("https://cassavabase.org", username = "your_username")
breedbase_programs(con)
breedbase_folders(con, program = "IITA")
breedbase_locations(con)

# Check the location and every entry and check before designing (or pass the
# design itself). All problems are listed together, with close matches:
breedbase_check(con, accessions = c(paste0("G", 1:108), paste0("C", 1:4)),
                location = "Ibadan", program = "IITA", folder = "AYT 2026",
                trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan")

# Checks everything (program, folder, location, accessions, trial name)
# without writing:
save_breedbase(rc, con, program = "IITA", folder = "AYT 2026",
               trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan", year = 2026, location = "Ibadan",
               create_folder = TRUE, dry_run = TRUE,
               description = "Advanced yield trial of 108 lines and 4 checks, Ibadan 2026")

# Saves after you type 'yes', then reads the plots back to verify:
saved <- save_breedbase(rc, con, program = "IITA", folder = "AYT 2026",
                        trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan", year = 2026,
                        location = "Ibadan", create_folder = TRUE,
                        description = "Advanced yield trial of 108 lines and 4 checks, Ibadan 2026")
saved$trial_page

# The folder is optional: without it the trial is saved directly in the
# breeding program.
save_breedbase(rc, con, program = "IITA", trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan",
               year = 2026, location = "Ibadan", dry_run = TRUE,
               description = "Advanced yield trial of 108 lines and 4 checks, Ibadan 2026")
```

Every entry and check must already exist as an accession in the database,
and the location must exist too. Run `breedbase_check()` before building the
design so that wrong names are fixed first; `save_breedbase()` repeats the
same checks and lists every problem together before writing anything.

The new trial needs a name (`trial_name`) and a description
(`description`, required: for example its purpose, material, location and
season; it is shown on the trial page in Breedbase), and every plot needs a
name that is unique in the whole database. By default plot names are made as
`trialName_accession_block_rep`:

```{r}
head(vapply(to_send$plots[[1]], function(p) p$observationUnitName, character(1)))
```

Choose another pattern with `plot_name_pattern` (fields `{trial}`,
`{accession}`, `{block}`, `{rep}`, `{plot}`, `{row}`, `{col}`), or give your
own names with `plot_names`, one per plot or the name of a column you added
to the field book:

```{r}
own <- save_breedbase(rc, trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan", year = 2026, location = "Ibadan",
                      plot_name_pattern = "{trial}_{plot}_r{row}c{col}", dry_run = TRUE,
                      description = "Advanced yield trial of 108 lines and 4 checks, Ibadan 2026")
head(vapply(own$plots[[1]], function(p) p$observationUnitName, character(1)))
```

## Saving phenotypic data to Breedbase

After harvest, the values go to the plots of the saved trial, matched by plot
name and trait name. The trait name is the one shown in Breedbase, with or
without its ontology id (`"fresh root yield"` or
`"fresh root yield|CO_334:0000013"`, as in a Breedbase phenotype download).
`phenotype_template()` gives a sheet with the plot names of the trial and an
empty column per trait:

```{r}
sheet <- phenotype_template(rc, trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan",
                            traits = c("fresh root yield", "dry matter content percentage"))
head(sheet)
```

Fill it in (here with simulated values; empty cells are skipped) and see what
would be sent, one row per value:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
sheet$`fresh root yield` <- round(rnorm(nrow(sheet), 25, 4), 1)
sheet$`dry matter content percentage` <- round(rnorm(nrow(sheet), 32, 3), 1)
obs <- save_breedbase_phenotypes(sheet, dry_run = TRUE)
head(obs)
```

With your database, every plot and trait is checked first and all problems
are listed together; then the values are saved in batches and read back.
Your account needs "submitter" rights. Long data (one row per value) works
too, and a time-stamp column allows repeated measurements of a trait:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
save_breedbase_phenotypes(sheet, con, dry_run = TRUE)   # check plots and traits
save_breedbase_phenotypes(sheet, con)                   # save and verify

long <- data.frame(plot_name = sheet$plot_name, trait = "fresh root yield",
                   value = sheet$`fresh root yield`, date = "2026-09-01 10:00:00")
save_breedbase_phenotypes(long, con, trait = "trait", value = "value", timestamp = "date")
```

## Saving analysis results to Breedbase

A first-stage analysis gives one value per field plot: the genotype's
adjusted mean plus the plot's residual, so blocks, rows, columns and (with
SpATS) the spatial trend are removed. It is saved on the plots of the field
trial as its own trait, so raw and adjusted values stay apart: the measured
trait composed with a statistic, as Breedbase does, e.g.
"fresh root yield|Adjusted Means from Spatial Correction using SpATS R". That
trait is found in Breedbase, or created (after you confirm) when it does not
exist yet; `breedbase_adjusted_trait()` shows it first. Your own traits can be
given with `as_trait`. A second-stage result, one value per genotype, is saved as a new
Breedbase analysis, as the Breedbase mixed-models tool does.

```{r}
field <- rc$design
field$yield <- sheet$`fresh root yield`[match(field$plots, sheet$plot_number)]
fit_yield <- analyze_augmented_row_column_design(field, "yield")

stage1 <- first_stage_values(fit_yield, rc, trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan", trait = "fresh root yield")
head(stage1)
stage2 <- second_stage_values(fit_yield, trait = "fresh root yield")
head(stage2)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
breedbase_adjusted_trait(con, "fresh root yield")   # the trait for adjusted values: exists?
save_breedbase_first_stage(stage1, con)              # creates it if needed, then saves
save_breedbase_analysis(stage2, con, analysis_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan_means", program = "IITA",
                        description = "Adjusted means, row-column model")
# Or the first stage as an analysis of the field plots ("Analysis of: plots"):
save_breedbase_analysis(stage1, con, analysis_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan_stage1", program = "IITA",
                        description = "Row-column model", level = "plot")
```

`first_stage_values()` works with every analysis of the package, including
the stage-1 fits per location of `analyze_augmented_prep_two_stage()` and
`analyze_resolvable_row_column()`.

## Add a second analyzed trait to an existing analysis

Analyze the second trait on the same field plots. In this example the dry
matter measurements are simulated; replace them with your field data:

```{r second-analyzed-trait}
set.seed(84)
field$dry_matter <- 32 + rnorm(nrow(field), sd = 2)
dm_fit <- analyze_augmented_row_column_design(field, "dry_matter")
dm_stage1 <- first_stage_values(dm_fit, rc, trial_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan",
  trait = "dry matter content percentage")
dm_stage2 <- second_stage_values(dm_fit, trait = "dry matter content percentage")
head(dm_stage2)
```

After saving the yield analyses shown above, append dry matter to those
same projects. Use `level = "plot"` for the first-stage plot analysis and
`level = "accession"` for the genotype-means analysis:

```{r append-analyzed-trait, eval = FALSE}
add_breedbase_analysis_values(dm_stage1, con,
  analysis_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan_stage1", level = "plot", dry_run = TRUE)
add_breedbase_analysis_values(dm_stage1, con,
  analysis_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan_stage1", level = "plot")

add_breedbase_analysis_values(dm_stage2, con,
  analysis_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan_means", level = "accession", dry_run = TRUE)
add_breedbase_analysis_values(dm_stage2, con,
  analysis_name = "AYT_2026_Ibadan_means", level = "accession")
```

The analysis must already contain those plots or accessions, and the new
trait must exist in Breedbase. Its connected dry run verifies the names and
values. Existing values for the same stock and trait require an explicit
`overwrite = TRUE` to replace them. Part A11 of `scripts/validate_designs.R`
demonstrates this with a second trait analyzed across all locations.

# Validation

The package source includes two scripts in `scripts/`:

* `validate_designs.R` is a step-by-step tour to run section by section in
  RStudio. It designs, plots, saves, simulates and analyses a trial of every
  kind and prints `[OK]` checks, including comparisons with the published
  examples (Table 2 of Piepho and Williams, 2016; Examples 1 and 3 of
  Williams, Piepho and Whitaker, 2011; Table 1 of Williams, John and
  Whitaker, 2006). A11 adds a second analyzed trait to the existing analyses;
  A12 is a standalone single-stage alternative (run A1-A6, then jump to
  A12). Part I covers agricolae designs. To analyze trials already in
  Breedbase, enable `read_breedbase_trials` and select
  `breedbase_analysis_route` (`"single"`, `"two_stage"` or `"both"`) in
  Setup, then run Part H. Subsequent traits are added to the same analysis
  projects.
* `run_all_checks.R` is the full automated test battery (thousands of
  checks against `lm()`, 'lme4', brute-force matrix algebra and the
  published tables, plus simulations of type I error, power and coverage).
  Run it from the package root with `Rscript scripts/run_all_checks.R`
  (add `--quick` for a shorter run, or `--only rrc,prep` for selected
  sections); it exits with an error if any check fails.

heterogeneity of variance. *Biometrika* 37, 308-312.
